introduction-the-precision-trap.core: Models are trained in FP32/BF16, but inference rarely needs that precision. Storing weights in INT8 or INT4 cuts memory 2–8× and speeds up inference, because LLM decoding is limited by how fast weights move from memory, often with minimal accuracy loss.

first_principles.problem: A 70B model in FP16 needs 140 GB of GPU memory and won't fit on one GPU.
truths: Neural nets tolerate small numeric noise.
Fewer bits mean less data to move.

analogy.title: A recipe in grams versus milligrams
analogy.story: Home cooking doesn't need milligram precision, and the dish tastes the same.
analogy.breaks: Some 'ingredients' (outlier weights, certain layers) really do need precision.

example.title: Sizing a 70B model
flow: INT4: 35 GB → fits one 48 GB GPU

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Serving cost cut by fitting fewer GPUs.

check.q: How much memory do 7B parameters need at INT4?

the-physics-of-quantization-mapping-the-.core: Quantization maps a float range [min, max] onto a small integer grid using a scale (and optionally a zero-point): q = round(x / scale) + zp. Symmetric schemes centre on zero; asymmetric schemes fit skewed ranges. Granularity (per-tensor, per-channel, per-group) controls how well the grid fits.

first_principles.problem: One huge outlier stretches the range so most values collapse onto a few integer levels.
truths: Finer granularity fits local ranges better.

analogy.title: Fitting an ocean into a cup with a ruler of marks
analogy.story: If the ruler must span a rare giant wave, everyday ripples all read as zero.
analogy.breaks: You can't use multiple rulers in the ocean, but per-group scales effectively do.

steps.label: Error
steps.detail: 0.004 rounding error, small relative to the value.

check.q: Why do outliers hurt per-tensor quantization?
check.a: They stretch the range, so the scale grows and normal values lose resolution.

calibration-finding-the-boundaries.core: Weights are fixed, so their ranges are known; activations depend on input. Calibration runs a representative sample of data through the model and records activation statistics, then picks clipping ranges (min-max, percentile, entropy/KL or MSE-optimal) that balance clipping error against rounding error.

first_principles.problem: Quantized activations clip badly on real traffic because ranges were set from random data.
truths: Clipping rare outliers improves typical precision.
Calibration data must look like production.
derivation: Choose **range method**: min-max, percentile (99.99%), KL, MSE.

analogy.title: Setting a camera's exposure from test shots
analogy.story: You take a few sample photos of the scene to choose settings before the real shoot.
analogy.breaks: Lighting changes during a shoot; production distribution shift may need recalibration.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Clip rare outliers for better overall precision.

check.q: Why not always use min-max calibration?
check.a: Rare outliers inflate the range and waste resolution for typical values.

ptq-vs-qat-when-to-quantize.core: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) quantizes a trained model using calibration only. It's fast and cheap, and works well at INT8 and, with methods like GPTQ/AWQ, at INT4 for LLMs. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) simulates quantization during training (fake-quant with straight-through gradients), so the model learns to tolerate it. It's costlier but recovers accuracy at low bit-widths.

first_principles.problem: PTQ to INT4 drops a vision model's accuracy by 6%, which is unacceptable.
truths: Models can adapt to noise if they see it in training.
derivation: If accuracy fails, apply **QAT** (fine-tune with fake-quant).

analogy.title: Translating a speech afterwards versus writing it for translation
analogy.story: Post-hoc translation is quick; writing with translation in mind avoids idioms that don't translate.
analogy.breaks: Speeches don't need gradients; QAT relies on the straight-through estimator to train through rounding.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Try cheap first; escalate only when needed.

check.q: What does QAT simulate during training?
check.a: The rounding and clamping of quantization (fake-quant), so the model learns weights robust to it.

hardware-acceleration-why-integers-are-c.core: Integer multipliers use far less silicon area and energy than floating-point ones, so GPUs and NPUs offer 2–4× more INT8/FP8 throughput than FP16. Fewer bytes also stretch memory bandwidth and cache. Speedups only appear if kernels and hardware actually support the format.

first_principles.problem: A model is quantized to INT4 but runs no faster because the runtime dequantizes to FP16 for every matmul.
truths: Multiplier cost grows roughly with bit-width squared.
Data movement costs more energy than arithmetic.
derivation: Match format to **hardware** (Tensor Core INT8/FP8, ARM dot-product).

analogy.title: Counting with whole coins versus measuring gold dust
analogy.story: Counting coins is quick and simple; weighing dust needs precise, slow scales.
analogy.breaks: Coins are always cheaper; integers only help if the hardware has fast integer paths.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Kernels matter as much as bits.

check.q: Why might a quantized model not run faster?
check.a: The runtime may lack optimised low-bit kernels and dequantize back to FP16, losing the benefit.

mixed-precision-quantization-not-all-lay.core: Layers differ in sensitivity: embeddings, first and last layers, attention outputs and outlier channels often degrade badly at low bits. Mixed precision measures per-layer sensitivity and keeps sensitive parts at FP16/INT8 while pushing robust layers to INT4, getting most of the savings with little loss.

first_principles.problem: Uniform INT4 breaks the model, but uniform INT8 doesn't save enough memory.
truths: A few layers hold most of the error.
derivation: **Profile** sensitivity (quantize one layer at a time and measure).
**Use** outlier handling (LLM.int8(), AWQ protects salient channels).

analogy.title: Packing a suitcase
analogy.story: Fold sweaters tightly but give the fragile glasses padding.
analogy.breaks: A suitcase has one constraint; mixed precision also has kernel-support constraints per format.

example.title: Sensitivity sweep
flow: Keep those at INT8, rest INT4

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Nearly INT4 size with near-INT8 quality.

check.q: Which parts of a model are commonly kept at higher precision?
check.a: Embeddings, the first and last (output) layers and outlier-heavy channels.
